column1: Reconstruct Wittgenstein's picture theory of meaning (Tractatus): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. The world is the totality of facts, and facts are combinations of simple objects in states of affairs (1-2). 2. A thought is a logical picture of facts, and a proposition expresses a thought (3-4). 3. A proposition pictures a possible state of affairs by sharing logical form with it: its names stand for objects, their arrangement for the objects' arrangement. 4. It is therefore bipolar: true if the state of affairs obtains, false if not, meaningful either way. Objection: The simple objects are never exhibited; determinacy of sense is demanded, not shown. Reply: Simples are a structural requirement of analysis, not an inventory to be produced on demand.

column1: Reconstruct the saying/showing argument and the ladder (Tractatus 4.1212, 6.54): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. A proposition pictures a fact by sharing logical form with it. 2. To state that form, a proposition would have to stand outside it, which is impossible: any statement already uses the form it would describe. 3. Therefore logical form shows itself in propositions but cannot be said (4.1212). 4. The Tractatus's own propositions are neither pictures nor tautologies, so by its standard they are elucidations: climb through them, recognize them as nonsensical, and throw away the ladder (6.54). Objection: Self-refuting: if the book is nonsense, nothing follows from it. Reply: Traditional readers: its truths are shown, not said. Resolute readers: nothing was ever asserted, so nothing is lost.

column1: Reconstruct the later Wittgenstein's argument against the Augustinian picture (PI sections 1-2, 43): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. The Augustinian picture: every word names an object, meaning is the object named, sentences are combinations of names (section 1). 2. The builders' language (section 2) functions completely - orders given and obeyed - yet its words work as calls within an activity, not names of correlated objects. 3. Actual words do irreducibly diverse jobs: ordering, describing, joking, praying (section 23). 4. Ostensive definition, the picture's mechanism, presupposes a practice already in place (sections 28-30). Conclusion: Meaning is not in general a naming relation. Objection: A straw man; Frege already distinguished sense from reference. Reply: The target is a governing picture, which survives inside sophisticated theories, the Tractatus included.

column1: State the meaning-as-use thesis exactly (PI section 43), with its textual basis, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: Section 43: 'For a large class of cases of the employment of the word "meaning" - though not for all - this word can be explained in this way: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.' Basis: the builders (section 2), where meaning is role in the activity; the toolbox (section 11), where words' functions differ as tools' do; the diversity of language-games (section 23). Objection: 'Use' is so broad the thesis is vacuous, and names of objects are a standing counter-example. Reply: The hedge is the point: it redirects attention from hidden correlates to observable practice; it does not legislate a new essence.

column1: Reconstruct the family resemblance argument against essentialism (PI sections 65-77): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. Essentialism: a concept such as game is understood only when a property common to all and only games is stated. 2. Surveying games (section 66) - competitive and solitary, skilled and luck-based - shows no such property; similarities appear, overlap, and drop out. 3. Yet speakers apply the concept and correct misuse without necessary and sufficient conditions. 4. A thread's strength lies in overlapping fibers, none running throughout (section 67). Conclusion: Some concepts are united by family resemblance, not essence. Objection: One messy case proves nothing about knowledge or number. Reply: The claim is methodological: look and see, case by case.

column1: Reconstruct the private language argument via the diary case (PI sections 243, 258, 265): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. Suppose a language whose words refer to sensations only the speaker can know (section 243), and a diarist fixing 'S' by inner concentration, resolving to reuse it for that sensation (section 258). 2. A sign has a use only if using it correctly differs from merely seeming to. 3. The only check on a later 'S' is the impression of sameness - itself what needs checking; memory cannot independently verify memory (section 265). 4. So whatever seems right is right: 'right' has no application. Conclusion: No criterion of correct use, no language. Objection: A castaway's diary seems meaningful. Reply: It borrows criteria from a public practice.

column1: Reconstruct the rule-following argument and its dissolution (PI sections 185, 201, 217): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. A pupil trained in the +2 series to 1000 continues 1004, 1008, claiming to go on in the same way (section 185): finite examples fit more than one rule. 2. If grasping a rule were having an interpretation, the interpretation - itself a sign - would need a further one to fix its application, endlessly (section 201). 3. So grasp cannot be interpretation all the way down. Conclusion: Grasping a rule is exhibited in practice - training, custom, technique; justifications end at bedrock (section 217). Objection (Kripke): No fact fixes which rule I meant. Reply: That demand is the rejected premise; within a practice, criteria already work.

column1: Reconstruct the beetle in the box argument (PI section 293): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. Everyone has a box only they can look into, calling its contents a 'beetle'. 2. No one can check another's box, nor their own contents against the word's public use. 3. The contents could change constantly, differ between people, or be absent - and the word's use would proceed unchanged. 4. So the private object, posited as the word's meaning, cancels out as irrelevant to the language-game. Conclusion: Sensation-words do not mean by naming private objects. Objection: This denies sensations exist. Reply: It denies a model of meaning, not pains; sensation-grammar rests on natural expression and public criteria (section 244).

column1: Reconstruct the aspect-seeing argument (PI Part II, section xi): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. The duck-rabbit can be seen as duck or as rabbit; when the aspect flips, everything changes, though the lines do not. 2. Not plain seeing: the object is unchanged, the experience transformed - and one can be told to try seeing it as a rabbit. 3. Not interpretation: the aspect dawns and one sees a rabbit immediately, without surveying neutral lines and inferring. 4. Positing an inner picture that changed while the outer stayed fixed explains nothing. Conclusion: Seeing-as straddles perception and thought; describe it fully and the puzzle dissolves. Objection: Some inner state must differ. Reply: Differing need not mean a pictorial mechanism explains it.

column1: Reconstruct the therapeutic conception of philosophy (PI sections 109, 116, 124, 133, 255): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. Problems arise when language goes on holiday (section 38): words lifted from their everyday work and idled into apparent depth. 2. They are not solved by new information or theory; nothing about use is hidden. 3. They are dissolved by arranging reminders of actual use - bringing words back from metaphysical to everyday use (section 116) - until the confusion loses its grip. Conclusion: Philosophy is therapy (sections 133, 255): it describes use, leaves everything as it is (section 124), and aims at peace from self-inflicted questions. Objection: Abdication: real questions go unanswered. Reply: Only one craving for theory is refused; the descriptions are checkable against your own use.

column1: Reconstruct the hinge argument of On Certainty (sections 341-343, 94-99): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. Doubting and testing have presuppositions: questions and tests depend on some propositions being exempt from doubt (sections 341-343). 2. Propositions like 'the earth existed long before my birth' are hinges: not known, not doubted, but standing fast - part of the world-picture, the river-bed of thoughts (sections 94-99). 3. Universal doubt would remove the conditions under which doubt makes sense. Conclusion: Moore's 'I know here is a hand' misplaces hinge propositions; the skeptic's global doubt is not false but senseless. Objection: This declines skepticism by relabeling. Reply: The claim is grammatical: 'doubt' lives inside a practice of grounds; outside it, the word idles.

column1: Reconstruct the Tractatus on the limits of language and the self (5.6-5.641, 6.421, 7): premises, conclusion, objection, reply.
column2: 1. The limits of my language mean the limits of my world (5.6): what propositions picture exhausts what can be thought clearly. 2. The metaphysical subject is not an item in the world but its limit, as the eye is not in its visual field (5.62-5.633). 3. Ethics lies outside the facts: 'Ethics cannot be put into words. Ethics is transcendental' (6.421). 4. So what matters most - the mystical, the world as a limited whole - shows itself and cannot be said (7). Objection: The Vienna Circle read this as contempt for ethics. Reply: The von Ficker letter reverses it: the unwritten part is the important one.

column1: Explain language-game in Wittgenstein's usage: what it is, and what work the section 23 list does.
column2: A language-game is language woven into an activity: giving orders and obeying them, describing, reporting, speculating, play-acting, guessing riddles, asking, thanking, cursing, greeting, praying (PI section 23). The list's motley diversity is itself the argument - no one activity on it is the essence of the others. Language-games are also objects of comparison: simplified models, like the builders of section 2, that illuminate actual language by similarity and dissimilarity. To imagine a language, section 19 adds, is to imagine a form of life: the game is never just words, but words at work in a shared practice.

column1: Explain form of life in Wittgenstein's usage, including the lion, and the scholarly caution about the term.
column2: A form of life is the shared background of practices and judgments within which speaking makes sense: 'to imagine a language means to imagine a form of life' (section 19). Agreement in language is agreement not in opinions but in judgments and in a form of life (sections 241-242). Hence: if a lion could talk, we could not understand him - his form of life is not ours. Caution: the term is used sparingly and never defined; its exact scope (biological, cultural, both) is debated. It marks where explanations run out - 'what has to be accepted, the given, is forms of life.'

column1: Explain why ostensive definition cannot found meaning (PI sections 28-30): the underdetermination point and stage-setting.
column2: Ostensive definition - pointing and saying 'this is called...' - looks like naming's foundation. What makes the pointing succeed? Point at a pencil and utter a word: has the learner been given the name of the shape, the color, the material, the number, or the pencil? The gesture underdetermines its lesson. Ostension works only because the learner already commands a stage-setting - some grasp of what kind of thing is being named, a language-game already in place. So it presupposes what it was meant to found. This is no skepticism about teaching children words, which succeeds daily; it locates the success in training into a practice.

column1: Explain logical form in the Tractatus: what it is, why it cannot be stated, and one thing that shows it.
column2: Logical form is the structure a proposition shares with the possible state of affairs it pictures - names arranged as the objects might be arranged (Tractatus 2.15-2.18, 4.12). It cannot itself be stated: a proposition describing the form would have to stand outside it, and any proposition already stands inside it. 'What can be shown, cannot be said' (4.1212). What shows it: meaningful propositions themselves, displaying the form in their working; and tautologies, which say nothing about the world but show the logical structure of language and world. Logical form is thus the Tractatus's central unsayable - and the pressure point where the ladder argument begins.

column1: Explain simple objects and elementary propositions in the Tractatus, and the two standing problems with them.
column2: Objects are the world's substance: simple, fixed, unalterable constituents whose combinations are states of affairs (2.01-2.027). Elementary propositions are the fully analyzed propositions whose names stand for objects; every proposition with sense is a truth-function of them. Two problems stand. Exhibition: no settled example of a simple object or elementary proposition was ever produced - they are demanded by the theory (without simples, sense is not determinate), not found. Independence: elementary propositions were to be logically independent, yet 'this is red all over' and 'this is green all over' exclude each other - Ramsey's color-exclusion problem, one pressure behind the 1929 turn.

column1: Explain the mystical in the Tractatus: what it is, what it is not, and the von Ficker letter's role.
column2: The mystical is the dimension outside the world of facts, hence outside factual speech: that the world exists at all, the world felt as a limited whole, ethics and aesthetics as transcendental (6.41-6.45, 6.421). Not hidden facts awaiting better words, and not a doctrine: it shows itself (6.522) precisely where saying stops. The 1919 letter to publisher Ludwig von Ficker is the key evidence for taking it seriously: the book's point was ethical, and it consists of the written part plus all he had not written - 'and it is precisely this second part that is the important one.' Silence here is reverence, not dismissal.

column1: Explain tautology and contradiction in the Tractatus, including the senseless/nonsensical distinction.
column2: Tautologies ('it is raining or it is not raining') and contradictions are propositions' limiting cases: true for every, or for no, state of affairs - so they say nothing and picture nothing. But they are not gibberish: Wittgenstein calls them senseless (sinnlos), not nonsensical (unsinnig). They belong to the symbolism as zero belongs to arithmetic, and they show the logical structure of language and world. Nonsense, by contrast, transgresses logical syntax - a sign given no meaning in some respect - and includes, on the book's own verdict, the Tractatus's propositions themselves (6.54). Keep the two apart: the ladder debate turns on it.

column1: Explain criteria in the later Wittgenstein's usage, and how criteria differ from symptoms.
column2: A criterion is a defeasible, practice-internal ground: part of what counts, grammatically, as settling that something is the case - as pain-behavior, in the right circumstances, is a criterion for pain. Criteria differ from symptoms, which are empirical correlations learned from experience: a falling barometer is a symptom of rain, not a criterion of it. Criteria can be defeated without ceasing to be criteria - circumstances can show the behavior was feigned - whereas a failed symptom just shows the correlation failed. The distinction matters for the private language argument: sensation-words rest on criteria - public, corrigible, built into the language-game - not on private samples.

column1: Explain bedrock and the turned spade (PI section 217): what runs out, and why that is not defeat.
column2: 'If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: "This is simply what I do."' (section 217). What runs out is justification: chains of reasons are internal to practices, and finally the explanation is the practice itself - training, custom, the technique of going on. Not defeat: justification was never owed to a standpoint outside all practices, and demanding one repeats the rule-following regress in a new costume. On Certainty applies the same structure to knowledge: doubt runs out at what stands fast. Bedrock names where justification lives, not where it fails.

column1: Explain agreement in judgments (PI sections 241-242) and its difference from agreement in opinions.
column2: Section 241: agreement in language is not agreement in opinions but in form of life. Section 242: communication requires agreement not only in definitions but in judgments. Opinions can be false - they are claims within the practice, assessable as true or false. Agreement in judgments is the prior concord in reactions - what counts as the same, as following a rule, as a reason - without which assessing opinions could not start. Not a vote, not a convention anyone signed: it shows in trained speakers' unhesitating going-on together. The community view of rule-following builds on this passage; individualist readers contest how much weight it bears.

column1: Explain Kripkenstein and the quus problem, with the labeling discipline the dossier requires.
column2: 'Kripkenstein' labels the possibly distinct philosopher of Kripke's Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language (1982). Quus: a function agreeing with plus on every sum so far computed but diverging on the next (57 + 68 = 5). The skeptical paradox: no fact about me - past use, dispositions, inner states - constitutes my having meant plus rather than quus. The skeptical solution: correctness is fixed by conditions under which a community licenses meaning-assertions. Discipline: quus and the solution are Kripke's construction, offered as the argument as it struck him; many scholars (Baker and Hacker prominently) reject it as exegesis - section 201's paradox is dissolved, not solved.

column1: Explain the resolute versus traditional reading of the Tractatus: the two verdicts and the key exhibits.
column2: Traditional (ineffability) reading - Hacker and others: the Tractatus conveys genuine truths about logical form and the mystical that can be shown but not said; the ladder is discarded, but something was learned on it. Resolute reading - Diamond and Conant: no ineffable truths exist; the propositions are plain nonsense, and therapy succeeds only when the reader stops salvaging doctrine from them. Key exhibits: 6.54, proposition 7, and the von Ficker letter, whose 'important unwritten part' cuts both ways. A middle range of readings exists. The dispute is live, not settled - and it decides the continuity question: one lifelong method, or a metaphysics surrendered.

column1: Explain perspicuous representation (PI section 122): what it is, what it replaces, and why it matters to the method.
column2: A perspicuous (surveyable) representation arranges the uses of our words so we can see the connections - and with them, the source of a philosophical confusion. Section 122 calls the concept one of fundamental significance: it characterizes the form of account we give, and how we look at things. It replaces the Tractatus's instrument, analysis: instead of digging beneath surface grammar to hidden logical form, the late work arranges what was always in view until the bewildering analogy loses its grip. Its product is understanding as seeing-connections, not information: nothing new is discovered, and the problem disappears. Liberation or abdication is the standing quietism debate.

column1: Explain aspect-blindness (PI Part II, section xi): the hypothetical condition, and what it is meant to illuminate.
column2: Aspect-blindness is Wittgenstein's hypothetical condition: an inability to experience the dawning of an aspect - to see the duck-rabbit flip from duck to rabbit while the drawing stays the same. The aspect-blind person can recognize and copy both figures and answer questions about them, but lacks the 'now it's a rabbit' experience and the concepts that hang on it (seeing-as, a likeness dawning). The construction illuminates by contrast what aspect-seeing is: not plain seeing (the object is unchanged) and not interpretation (the aspect is seen, not inferred). Wittgenstein likens the deficiency to color-blindness or the absence of absolute pitch - a thought experiment, not a diagnosis.

column1: Explain the duck-rabbit distinctions: dawning versus continuous seeing, and seeing-as versus seeing-that (PI Part II, section xi).
column2: The duck-rabbit, adapted from a puzzle picture popularized by psychologist Joseph Jastrow, can be seen as a duck (facing left) or a rabbit (facing right). Continuous seeing is having only ever seen it one way; the dawning of an aspect is the flip - drawing unchanged, experience transformed. Seeing-that reports a fact and is checkable; seeing an aspect is describable only by comparison ('now it's a rabbit') and partly obeys the will: you can be told to see it as a rabbit, and try, and succeed. Seeing-as thus straddles perception and thought; inserting an inner picture to explain it repeats, for perception, the private-object picture.

column1: Explain 'language goes on holiday' (PI section 38) and the idling engine: the diagnosis these images carry.
column2: Confusion arises, section 38 says, when language is like an engine idling - running but doing no work - when language 'goes on holiday.' Words lifted from their home activities keep their familiar look and lose their function: 'meaning', 'know', 'object', 'I' treated as names of exotic items, though in their home games they do quite different jobs. The diagnosis sets the therapy: do not theorize about the idle word; return it to work - bring it back from its metaphysical to its everyday use (section 116) - and describe the games where it earns its keep. Self-diagnosis included: the Tractatus's fully analyzed proposition is language idling at maximum polish.

column1: Explain blurred edges (PI sections 69-71): why a concept without sharp boundaries can still be a concept.
column2: Section 71: 'the concept "game" is a concept with blurred edges' - and a blurred photograph is still a picture, usable where sharpness is not needed. Sections 69-70: a boundary can be drawn for a special purpose, but the drawing shows neither that the concept was defective before nor a line already there; tennis has no rule for how high the ball may be thrown, and is a game all the same. Usability is purpose-relative: speakers applied the concept, extended it, and corrected misuse long before any definition. The essentialist demand - no understanding without necessary and sufficient conditions - is a requirement we impose, not one concepts secretly meet.

column1: Explain world-picture in On Certainty (sections 94-95, 162): what it is, and how it is acquired.
column2: A world-picture (Weltbild) is the inherited background against which I distinguish the true from the false: not single propositions but a system of convictions, a nest in which each is held by the whole (On Certainty sections 94-95, 141-144, 162). 'I did not get my picture of the world by satisfying myself of its correctness... No: it is the inherited background' (section 94). It is acquired by upbringing and absorption - swallowed down in childhood belief - and shows itself in action rather than assertion. Individual propositions within it can change; the picture itself changes slowly, like a river-bed (section 97), and mostly elsewhere than at the point under test.

column1: Explain why, for the late Wittgenstein, doubt presupposes certainty (On Certainty, sections 115, 341-343).
column2: 'If you tried to doubt everything you would not get as far as doubting anything. The game of doubting itself presupposes certainty' (section 115). Doubt is a move inside a practice: it needs grounds, checking-methods, and a background standing fast while the doubted item is tested - the hinges of sections 341-343. A child learns by believing; doubt comes after belief, parasitic on it. The skeptic's universal doubt fails not by being false but by failing to get started: it uses doubt's language-game while denying the conditions giving the game its sense. Moore's certainty and the skeptic's doubt are mirror errors: both treat hinges as ordinary claims.

column1: Explain grammatical versus empirical propositions in the later Wittgenstein, and why the boundary is itself instructive.
column2: A grammatical proposition articulates a rule of use - part of how a word is employed ('a rod has a length') - where an empirical proposition states a fact, assessable within the rules. The distinction works hard: pseudo-problems often come from mistaking grammar for fact, demanding evidence for what is really a rule of description. But the boundary is no wall: On Certainty's river-bed (section 97) has propositions hardening into channels and channels liquefying into empirical claims over time, and one sentence can function either way in different games. For a disputed sentence ask not first 'is it true?' but 'what work is it doing here?'

column1: Explain the Nachlass problem and the two-Wittgensteins framing: what is editorial, and what hangs on it.
column2: Wittgenstein published one philosophy book in his lifetime (the Tractatus, 1921/1922). Everything else - Investigations (1953), Blue and Brown Books, Zettel, On Certainty, Culture and Value - was assembled by his executors (Anscombe, Rhees, von Wright) from a Nachlass of some twenty thousand pages, in editorially arranged selections. What hangs on it: appeals to 'what Wittgenstein really thought' from notebooks are methodologically contested, and Part I of the Investigations - prepared by him for publication - outranks Part II and the clippings. The early/late split is also a scholarly framing, not his title: the break is real (the Preface: grave mistakes), and so is the continuity (philosophy as activity, 4.112).

column1: Explain section 124 - philosophy 'leaves everything as it is' - and the two extensions of it that must be flagged.
column2: 'Philosophy may in no way interfere with the actual use of language; it can in the end only describe it... It leaves everything as it is' (section 124). The claim governs philosophy and language: no legislating grammar, no reforming usage from theory, no explaining use away by deeper mechanisms; it describes. Flag two extensions. Political quietism: Gellner's Words and Things (1959) charges ordinary-language philosophy with sanctifying usage and evading criticism - but section 124 concerns usage and adds no premise about reform generally. Anti-theory absolutism: the therapy works by concrete, checkable reminders of use; a 'therapeutic' shrug that cannot point to its example is incantation, not method.
